speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview of Lady Corb was made at St. Mary's, Idaho on June 19, 1975 by Irma Wood. I guess we're ready. Let's see it. Isn't the wig on? Wait just a minute, Abby. That's okay now. Well, I have many advantages of living as close to town as I do, only a quarter of a mile from town. And especially since they have paid the road out to my house, it's almost like living in town. And I have this wonderful valley to look at. I call it my Green Valley. Of course, there are many other homes out in the valley. They are beginning to subdivide some of the valley. And so it really isn't as much my Green Valley anymore as it used to be. I wouldn't trade my wife in the country for any place in town. I never have ever wanted to live in town. I grew up in a city and never liked it, even at that time, although we lived sort of on the edge of town. But every chance I got, I went to the country to my uncles and my aunts and my grandmothers and would spend the whole summer with them whenever I had the chance. And my mother let me go quite often because when I was three, I had the measles. And my father always said they settled in my heart, but they gave me rheumatic fever and a bad heart also. A bad heart came from the rheumatic fever. And so I was quite a sickly young child. And so to get me away from my brothers and sisters, my mother would send me to those other places where there weren't other children. And so I enjoyed this life on the farm and had all the good, wholesome farm products and all the milk I could drink and things every summer. And right now I live all alone. My husband has passed on since he left me many years ago. And my children have grown. I have two boys. And my children have grown, so I live here on my place all by myself. I have a big nine-room home, and it got too big for me by myself, so I made me a small apartment in another building that I had on the place. And it's very comfortable for me, and I rent my big house. I made a duplex out of my large house, and so I have income that way to help me, and it's very providing. Did you want to say something about your garden? Oh, so now I have nothing to worry about financially. I, like I say, I have my place rented, and I worked for a number of years after my husband passed away for the Potlatch Timber Company. I worked for them in their camps, and mostly up at Camp 44 near Avery, Idaho, and enjoyed it very much up there. I was part of the kitchen help. Sometimes I was first cook. Sometimes I was second cook. Sometimes I was baker, and sometimes I waited on the tables. It's garden on where we needed the help the most, that wherever I worked. And if we had somebody that could take over in the kitchen better, the help, the work there was quite heavy, the big pots and pans. When I first went to work for Potlatch, we had 150 men to feed three times a day. And of course, it was very heavy work, and everything was done by hand at that time, although we did have electric lights, but we didn't have any electrical equipment. But in later years, they brought in electrical equipment for us, so we didn't have to cut our bacon by hand. We didn't have to slice any meat by hand after that. And we also had a machine to do our mixing, a mixing machine. We mixed our bread and all of our cakes and our cookie doughs and things like that. Everything that we could mix went into our mixer, a large mixer, and we mixed everything that way, which was very nice and helped us very, very much. But we baked everything that went on the table, and we would have hot rolls every evening. We baked all of our own bread for the men's use at the table and for their lunches. We had all that lunch meat to slice, and we'd put it on platters and put it out in the mornings, and the men would come in and build their own lunches. And we had coffee sitting there for them to fill the thermos bottles. They'd fill the thermos bottles, make up their own sandwiches. We had plenty of sweets there for them to have. They could have donuts. They could have pie, cake, cookies, or sometimes we even had crullers for them. And they would build these lunches, and always fresh fruit. They had fresh fruit to eat also in their lunches. Beside, we would have canned fruit, and if they had a little jar, they could fill their little jar and have canned fruit. And then we, they would do this in the morning before breakfast. Then they would come in and eat their breakfast, and oh, the stacks of hot cakes they would eat. Then we had such a good time in the camps when we weren't so busy working, why we'd take time off almost every day and go out in the woods a little bit. There's some times when the rest of them would pick huckleberries all around me, and I'd lay on a great big log and have a little nap or just rest. I'd be tired and I would rest, and the rest of them. But just to be out in the woods is what I loved to be. I could have stayed at home in my little house that the company provided for all of us. And we had families in the camp, and we were just like one great big family there, the women and the children. And we'd go on picnics and go fishing. And then in the fall, several of us would hunt together, and in the spring we would mushroom together. And we just really had a good time all the years that I spent in the camps, which were 25 years that I spent in the potlatch camps. Then when potlatch closed their camps, I went looking for work, and I was able to secure a job as first cook in the student union building at Washington State University at Pullman, Idaho. And I stayed there until I retired. So I built me up a good social security, and with my social security and my rent money, I am able to get by real well now. And then I have a small acreage, well, I have sold part of the land I did right away when I first became a widow. I knew I couldn't farm all of it, and so I sold all my bottom land that was under the dike, and I sold all of that. And so I just have 30 acres left, and I had some hay land then to sell each year, the hay off of. And when I was a child, my brothers and sisters and I, we used to have lots of fun. My folks couldn't afford, there was four of us, my folks could not afford to have everything for all of us. So one brother got a pair of boxing gloves, and we would all put on the boxing gloves and take turns and boxing. And we had one pair of skates between us, and we'd take turns on our skates. We had one bicycle between us, and we'd take turns on that bicycle. And we had a baseball outfit, and we would play baseball out in the street, and my father would play with us. He was quite a man to play with the children, and he always looked after us, and we children always stayed at home. We weren't allowed to go anywhere, but anybody could come, and he didn't care how many came to our house. They could come and play with us, and so it seemed like I was the only girl when I get a little bigger, or when I was strong enough, I could go out for a few hours with them. I would be out, and I'd be the only girl with all the rest would be boys and my dad. But I had a lot of fun anyway. And we, we would play, and nobody ever bickered too much or anything about it was their turn to have this or their turn to have that. It seemed like we always got along all right. But when it came to ice skates, I don't know how come we had more ice skates, but my two brothers and myself each had a pair of ice skates. And we could go ice skating by ourselves, but in those days ice skates are not what they are now. We had ice skates that we had to fasten onto what shoes we had. We didn't have, nobody had shoe skates in those days. And so those little skates I guess didn't cost very much money. They seemed to me like they only cost about a dollar, dollar and a half, or something like that. And we were able to get them, probably some of them were hand-me-downs from somebody else. Then we used to go to school. Our school was five blocks away. My brothers and my sisters and I, we'd go to school and have, being a little rheumatic, I used to get arthritis a lot. And sometimes I'd get it in my legs, one leg or the other, and then I couldn't walk very well. So they'd take me by the hand and start running and I'd have to go on one leg all the way to school. But I wanted to go to school. I didn't want to miss any more school than I had to. And I used to cry when I'd be sick and couldn't go to school. I'd cry. And then after I would have been, I guess I was about in the third grade or something, where they had a teacher come around to teach the children that couldn't get into school. So I was able always to make my grades. Sometimes I passed on what they called on time, and I'd have six weeks for them to make up their mind if I was going to be able to make my grade or not. But I always made it. They never put me back once. And then my little brother was so smart that he kept skipping until finally he was up with me. But he kind of lived to regret it. Here not very long ago, we had a family reunion, and he was telling our nephew, if it hadn't been for your father, he said, I never would have passed because he said, I skipped all my fractions. And he said, I didn't know them. And I never would have, but my older sister had married, and her husband was a timekeeper. And he knew his arithmetic, and he taught us both arithmetic. And Howard to this day is, well, he's retired now, but he taught all his life in one school. He never went from the very first school. He was at the Jefferson High School in Dallas, Texas. All of his teaching years he taught high school there. And he never forgot how our brother-in-law helped us through our arithmetic, and especially him. And of course, my father being a minister, we had many activities in the church. We had church socials. We all sang in the choir, although I can't carry a tune in a bucket, but I sang in the choir. My brothers played in the orchestra. My sister would play the piano sometimes. She always played the piano at Sunday school. Then there would be someone else take over the piano for the orchestra sometimes. But we always had an orchestra at home. And the different ones in the neighborhood that played instruments, they would come down at least once a week and play. And so much fun that we had around the piano in the evening, or sometimes it would be early. Of course, it was always early in the evening, but sometimes it would be in the afternoon they would come and congregate. Such times we had playing, and we never thought of money. Had very little money. We never even wanted to go with money. I can remember when my mother would give us a quarter, and we would go out to a place called Capitol Beach, and she'd give us a quarter and a streetcar check. And we'd stay out there all day and have a good time, and then get on the streetcar because we couldn't spend our streetcar check for anything only to come home on. So she knew we would always get home all right. And then when I got through high school, I went on to the university. My health was so much better by then. And during my high school years, my health began to improve quite considerably. And I went on and went two years to the University of Nebraska, and then I went teaching, and I taught two years. And during that two years, well, in fact, during the first year, I met a man, and the more I saw of him, of course, the more I liked him. So finally at the end of my second teaching year, we decided that we would get married. So on June 18, 1924, we were married. And my girlfriend wanted to get married at the same time, but they wanted to get married in Constable Bluffs, Iowa, she and her friend. So we all went over there and had a double ring ceremony in Constable Bluffs, Iowa. And we had so much fun because the minister's name was Ringer. And we kind of laughed over that because we said he had a double ringer that day. And then the other couple, the man's name was Victor Slusselman. And the minister stumbled over his name. And I giggled, and then my husband giggled, and my girlfriend frowned at us. And even Victor giggled when he slussed over his name. But at the time, Victor had a cough, and it wasn't long before he was bed-fast with TB, and he didn't live very long after that, which was a very sad thing for all of us. And my cousin told me, she said, Well, I hate to say it, but there always is one, when you have a double wedding, one who is never happy if something happens to one of the couples. So I was real glad in a way that it was them, although I felt sorry for them. I was glad it wasn't me that had the bad luck. And then I was married a year and three months and a little over, and then I had a baby son. And he was so beautiful, I thought, so tiny. And the doctor I had been going to, the specialist, was out of town the night that he was born. And we had to have a strange man, strange doctor come. And I didn't even make it to the hospital because I had just seen the doctor two days before, and he said it would be all of two weeks. And so when I took sick, we didn't know what was the matter exactly. And my husband says, Something you ate. So I stayed home and waited for the doctor to come. And when he came, I was holding my baby to keep him from being born. So the doctor said, Well, mother, he said, Well, we're going to have a baby right now. And I said, Oh, no, I have to go to the hospital. And he said, Oh, but you can't go to the hospital. So my baby boy was born at home, and I never made it to the hospital. And the next day, he found a nurse for me and sent her over to our house. And she stayed with me for ten days those days. You always stayed in bed ten days with your baby. And then you wasn't able to get up and do very much. And so I found out when I had that baby that I would never have any more children. So right away, we didn't want to raise this boy by ourselves. So we tried to find another boy or another child. And as it turned out, it happened to be a boy. And he was older than our boy. He was ten months older than our boy. But we were able to get him. So the two were almost like twins. And what one did, the other one did. And they got along beautifully. There was never any dissension among them, no fights. Now, when I was growing up, once in a while, we kids used to bicker and fight. And I remember my dad, Jet, making us kiss and make up. And you know, that was the worst thing we could do, is kiss each other and make up. Then... Not knowing anything about childbirth, and then I've never been around a brand-new baby but one since then. And one of my tenants had a little baby girl. And she came home from the hospital the very next day. I guess she was in the hospital one full day. And then the morning of the next day, after that second day, after the baby was born, she came home. And I was working at camp, and I came home from camp and went over to see her. And she said, Oh, I'm so glad you're here. You can bathe the baby. Well, I hadn't even bathed my own baby when it was that young. But I bathed the baby, and I was frightened almost to death. Fear I wouldn't do it just right and something would go wrong. But Sally lived through my bathing all right. And she was all right. And her mother had varicose veins and had to stay in bed for a while. So she depended on the neighbors to come in and bathe the baby each day. And the lady that lived in the upstairs apartment, I'd seen that they got something to eat. And I guess that Mrs. Hartman got up out of bed a little bit too, did a little bit. But she had to spend most of her time in bed until her veins got a little bit better. Then this boy that we raised, I sent him on to the university. My husband had passed away before he got through the university. He had only started just within his freshman year when my husband passed away. And so I finished sending him to the university. Of course, the war had come on, and he'd gone to war. Both of my boys were in the war. So my own son went as a sailor, and my foster son went as a soldier boy. And he was over in France and Germany. And when he came home, he wanted to go on to school. And so we seemed to it that he got, of course, he got some on his GI loan. And that helped immensely. And then by my working for Potlatch Forest, I was able to help him through the school. And he became a teacher. And at this time, he is teaching at Corvallis, Oregon, in the high school, one high school there. And called the Corvallis High School. They have three high schools there. And he will be 51 this November. And he has four children, two boys and two girls. And I received word today that his second son just got married. And they are a beautiful Christian family. They've all been saved. And the girl that Clayton just married also gave her life to the Lord. So we are very happy for them. And the oldest boy is married to a school teacher. And so they seem to be getting along just fine. And his oldest daughter doesn't want to go to school. She's through high school, but she doesn't want to go on to the university. And she's following in my footsteps, I guess. She's got a job of cooking, helping in the kitchen and helping cook at the country club there at Corvallis. And she likes her job immensely. And she went to work there the latter part of March. And she has already saved over $400. So we think she's doing just marvelously. Then the little girl is 13 years old. And she, of course, is getting along just fine. She has a bicycle she rides. And one of her girlfriends that lives quite close has a horse. And they get on this horse and ride and have quite a good time on that. And for relaxation, I love to fish and hunt and work in my garden and my yard. I was thinking, wondering if you wanted to say anything about your bears and things up at camp. Well, up at camp, I have many pictures that I took of the animals up there. And while I was cooking in the camps, I was able to shoot a real nice bear. I killed many bears. But I have one that I killed just before Thanksgiving one year. And it was right in the prime. And I was able to have a bear rug made out of it. And it's a beautiful black bear rug. And it measured 6 feet from tip to tip. And it's a beautiful thing. And then I have so many pictures of the moose and the elk and the deer. And little chipmunks. I even like to take pictures of them and watch them. They're so cute. And I certainly enjoyed my life in the woods. I wouldn't take those years that I worked in the woods for anything that I can think of. And I get lonesome for them now. And I go out in the woods in my car and sit there and get out and run around in the woods. But the animals aren't as plentiful as they used to be up here. We can go and stay all day in the woods now and never see one animal. Okay, thank you.
